2026-10-11: every existing test re-run after the changes with the same results as the baseline. Nothing here has been compared with the real robot

limits: No number of the physics model was measured on the robot: mass, inertia, friction, motor force, tyre stiffness, fan force and sensor noise are all guesses.

The simulated firmware runs the tuning values in the code, which since 2026-10-11 are the set saved on the robot on 2026-10-10. If the team saves new values on the robot, the code and the simulation fall behind until they are copied over.
The force model has no sideways sliding, no weight shift under acceleration and no airflow; the fan is a fixed extra downward force.

With the tuning the code had before 2026-10-11, the force-model robot broke the lab's limits on 3 of 5 mazes; with the robot's saved set, on 0 of 5, and on 1 of 51 across all 17 scenarios. Passing nearly everything may mean the scenarios are too gentle at these speeds, not that the robot is safe.
The front level is never measured in a simulated maze, so the front-wall stop and the safety supervisor's front check do not act there.
Wall calls are scored for the 90 degree and front sensors at cell centres only; the 45 degree look-ahead is not scored, and it is switched off in the firmware.
Collisions test a circle around the axle (43.75 mm in the lab, 40 mm in the regression tests), not the robot's real outline.

Curves and diagonals are simulated for speed runs only (moves=1, moves=2); the search always turns on the spot. With diagonals the closest approach left no margin (50.1 mm against a limit of 49.75) on a model that cannot slide sideways.
Control-loop timing is not simulated: every tick takes no time.
